Contents of https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/menasource/sisi-egypt-election-gaza-third-term/:
[MENASource](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/content-type/menasource/)
December 7, 2023

[Shahira Amin](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/expert/shahira-amin/)

Egyptians [head](https://www.dailysabah.com/world/mid-east/egyptians-to-head-to-polls-for-presidential-elections-on-dec-10-12) to the polls from December 10-12 to cast their ballots in a presidential election that analysts say is certain to [guarantee](https://www.i24news.tv/en/news/middle-east/north-africa/1696268862-egyptians-rally-in-cairo-for-sisi-s-potential-third-term-bid) a third term for incumbent Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, who has been in power for nearly a decade. Skeptics lament the outcome of the upcoming election. At the same time, some activists have called for the cancellation of the vote, [arguing](https://twitter.com/ghadasha/status/1700607370622034294) that it is “a waste of taxpayers’ money” at a time when Egypt faces a severe economic crisis.

Israel’s war in the neighboring Gaza Strip, meanwhile, has [overshadowed](https://www.agenzianova.com/en/news/egitto-la-guerra-a-gaza-oscura-le-elezioni-presidenziali/) the upcoming election. Pre-occupied with the developments unfolding next door, many Egyptians have put their domestic issues and economic woes on the back burner for the time being. Giant portraits of a smiling Sisi plastered on billboards and hanging from lampposts in the main squares as well as across the streets of the capital Cairo are the only [reminders](https://www.thenationalnews.com/mena/egypt/2023/11/30/egyptians-fixated-on-gaza-war-see-el-sisi-posters-as-reminder-of-upcoming-vote/) that an election is taking place.

Learning from the mistakes of the last presidential election held in 2018—which at the time was denounced as “farcical” by Egyptian and international human rights organizations—Egyptian authorities are seeking to give some semblance of a democratic, multi-candidate election this time around. In the previous election, Sisi had run against a little-known challenger—[Moussa Mostafa Moussa](https://english.ahram.org.eg/NewsContent/1/1187/289022/Egypt/-Presidential-Elections--/Egyptian-presidential-hopeful-Moussa-Mostafa-Mouss.aspx), an architect-turned-politician who had [endorsed](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2018/3/23/egypt-election-is-mousa-mostafa-mousa-a-puppet-of-sisi) a Sisi candidacy. Moussa became the sole candidate against Sisi after several serious presidential hopefuls [dropped out](https://www.dw.com/en/egypt-last-serious-challenger-to-el-sissi-drops-out-of-presidential-race/a-42297171) of the race or were arrested on what Amnesty International described as “[trumped up](https://www.amnesty.or.jp/en/news/2018/0131_7265.html)” charges.

In the upcoming election, Sisi is competing against [three](https://www.newarab.com/news/four-candidates-announced-egypts-presidential-race) rival candidates from various political parties. However, the fact that all three are non-military men has caused some Egyptians to doubt the election. The Egyptian military, the institution from which every modern Egyptian leader has emerged—save for the former Muslim Brotherhood President Mohamed Morsi, who was [ousted](https://www.france24.com/en/20130703-liveblog-egypt-brink-morsi-deadline-looms-tahrir-protests-army-video) by the army in 2013—has made clear it is unwilling to [cede](https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/frontline/article/inside-the-egyptian-militarys-brutal-hold-on-power/) power to a civilian government.

Egyptians might have believed the elections were genuine if it had not been for the fact that one serious competitor—[Ahmed el-Tantawy](https://english.ahram.org.eg/NewsContent/1/140/510209/Egypt/Presidential-Elections-/Former-MP-Ahmed-Tantawi-ends-presidential-election.aspx), a former member of parliament and former head of the leftist Karama (Dignity) Party—was forced to [end](https://english.ahram.org.eg/NewsContent/1/140/510209/Egypt/Presidential-Elections-/Former-MP-Ahmed-Tantawi-ends-presidential-election.aspx) his presidential bid just hours before the [deadline](https://english.ahram.org.eg/News/509004.aspx) for announcing candidacy on October 14. Tantawy had [failed](https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20231013-main-opposition-hopeful-abandons-run-for-egypt-presidency) to collect the required number of endorsements to allow him to submit his bid formally. Many of Tantawy’s supporters cited [harassment](https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20231013-main-opposition-hopeful-abandons-run-for-egypt-presidency)—and some even physical [assault](https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20231013-main-opposition-hopeful-abandons-run-for-egypt-presidency)—by pro-government mobs at public notaries when supporters tried to register their support for his candidacy—allegations that have been [denied](https://english.ahram.org.eg/NewsContentP/1/510209/Egypt/Former-MP-Ahmed-Tantawi-ends-presidential-election.aspx) by members of the National Elections Authority overseeing the elections.

Dozens of Tantawy’s supporters have been [arrested](https://www.hrw.org/news/2023/05/05/egypt-mass-arrests-target-family-supporters-ex-mp) in recent weeks and face charges of “falsifying” their endorsements for his candidacy. Several of Tantawy’s family members have also been arrested and detained. Meanwhile, Tantawy and twenty-two members of his campaign are [facing trial](https://www.newarab.com/news/former-egypt-presidential-hopeful-tantawi-face-trial) on the accusation of “inciting others to influence the conduct of the electoral process.” However, Egyptian rights organizations have rebuffed the charge. In a joint statement released on November 12, the rights groups [condemned](https://www.cfjustice.org/egypt-al-tantawy-prevented-from-running-for-presidency-and-referred-to-trial-underscoring-illegitimacy-of-upcoming-elections/) “the escalating retaliatory practices” against the opposition politician, which they said were meant to stop Tantawy from exercising his legitimate right to run in the presidential race.

[Abdel Sanad Yamama](https://english.ahram.org.eg/News/509859.aspx), who heads Egypt’s [oldest](https://www.arabnews.com/node/2323901/middle-east) political party, Al Wafd, was the first to [announce](https://english.ahram.org.eg/News/503245.aspx) his candidacy. He has said in interviews that he was confident that his party’s mass appeal would win him votes.

In the early days after its establishment in the wake of the [1919 popular uprising](https://enterprise.press/archive-wealth/look-back-egypts-roaring-20s/) against British rule, Al Wafd was a liberal [opposition force](https://www.france24.com/en/20190319-egypts-historic-wafd-party-eclipsed-under-sisis-rule) with a massive following. Over the years, however, the party has [lost](https://www.france24.com/en/20190319-egypts-historic-wafd-party-eclipsed-under-sisis-rule) its luster and clout and seen its popularity dwindle. In the current [stifling](https://timep.org/2018/06/22/egypts-party-consolidation-and-the-stifling-of-pluralism/) political climate, it has been weakened even further and dismissed by some [critics](https://www.independent.co.ug/egypts-historic-wafd-party-eclipsed-under-sisis-rule/) as “irrelevant.”

One analyst, who prefers to remain anonymous, told me that Yamama’s presidential bid was “little more than window dressing,” meant to create a more favorable impression of the elections.

“A Wafd candidate will stand little to no chance of winning the election against Sisi,” Hassan Nafaa, a political science professor at Cairo University, was [quoted](https://www.france24.com/en/20190319-egypts-historic-wafd-party-eclipsed-under-sisis-rule) as saying by France24 in 2019.

Moreover, Yamama does not have the full backing of his party. Internal [divisions](https://english.ahram.org.eg/News/503665.aspx) persist within Al Wafd, with some members throwing their weight behind [Fouad Badrawi](https://english.ahram.org.eg/News/503665.aspx), a former member of parliament and a member of Al Wafd Supreme Council who had sought to be the party’s presidential nominee.

[Farid Zahran](https://english.ahram.org.eg/News/508848.aspx), the head of the leftist Social Democratic Party, is another presidential hopeful and, perhaps, the best-known of the three rival candidates running against Sisi. He has gained recognition within intellectual circles for his political contributions, which have been published in various local newspapers and on news sites. Zahran was [appointed](https://english.ahram.org.eg/News/510268.aspx) by President Sisi as a member of the Egyptian Senate in 2021, possibly to reward him for backing the 2013 overthrow of the then-Muslim Brotherhood president by military-backed protests.

Dismissing criticism of the election as a theatrical farce, he recently told the independent *Al Masry Al Youm* [website](https://www.almasryalyoum.com/news/details/3042024) that “my credentials do not permit me to be part of a staged election,” insisting that his candidacy was based on his party’s decision to field a candidate that could unite opposition forces and garner their support.

Zahran advocates for a mixed system of governance that grants equal powers to parliament and the head of state and a free market economy as the only way to achieve social justice. He also promises to [prioritize](https://english.ahram.org.eg/News/509520.aspx) the release of political detainees and prisoners of conscience if he were to win the election and vows to diminish the role of the state in the economy by relinquishing ownership of strategic assets like the Suez Canal and the Iron and Steel Company. But his pledges have failed to entice even the young revolutionaries who led the 2011 uprising against former President Hosni Mubarak and have decried the arbitrary detentions of dissenters and the state monopoly over the economy. Many activists have dismissed Zahran’s campaign promises as “hollow” and tell me that his pledges are no more than “empty campaign talk.”

[Hazem Omar](https://nabd.com/s/128843875-cbc0e7/%D8%AD%D8%A7%D8%B2%D9%85-%D8%B9%D9%85%D8%B1-%D9%8A%D9%83%D8%B4%D9%81-%D8%B9%D9%86-%D8%A3%D9%87%D9%85-%D9%85%D9%84%D8%A7%D9%85%D8%AD-%D8%A8%D8%B1%D9%86%D8%A7%D9%85%D8%AC%D9%87-%D9%84%D8%A5%D8%B5%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%AD-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AA%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%8A%D9%85-%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B5%D8%AD%D8%A9), an engineer and member of the little-known People’s Republican Party, formed in 2012, meanwhile, vows to [reform](https://nabd.com/s/128843875-cbc0e7/%D8%AD%D8%A7%D8%B2%D9%85-%D8%B9%D9%85%D8%B1-%D9%8A%D9%83%D8%B4%D9%81-%D8%B9%D9%86-%D8%A3%D9%87%D9%85-%D9%85%D9%84%D8%A7%D9%85%D8%AD-%D8%A8%D8%B1%D9%86%D8%A7%D9%85%D8%AC%D9%87-%D9%84%D8%A5%D8%B5%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%AD-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AA%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%8A%D9%85-%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B5%D8%AD%D8%A9) the education and healthcare systems. His campaign platform is again meant to appeal to Sisi’s opponents, who have criticized him for prioritizing infrastructure [mega-projects](https://carnegieendowment.org/sada/79625) with questionable economic benefits over education and healthcare.

During a televised [interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?si=uRZCjGOyevyvQnPs&v=NFG0uSLNXk0&feature=youtu.be) on the talk show *El Hekaya*, broadcast on the Saudi-owned satellite channel MBC Masr on November 28, Omar sought to [assure](https://www.youtube.com/watch?si=uRZCjGOyevyvQnPs&v=NFG0uSLNXk0&feature=youtu.be) skeptical Egyptians that “your vote counts as it will determine who will become the president of Egypt.” He cautioned against voter apathy, telling viewers that boycotting the elections and calling them a sham is “inappropriate.”

Voter turnout was markedly low at around [40 percent](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/new-atlanticist/in-egypt-voter-turnout-falls-short/) and [47.5 percent](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2014/jun/03/abdel-fatah-al-sisi-presidential-election-vote-egypt) in the last two elections held in 2018 and 2014 respectively. Many Egyptians failed to show up at polling stations, believing that the results were pre-determined. A repeat of the [voter apathy](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2018/mar/26/egypt-election-polls-open-amid-concerns-over-voter-apathy) witnessed in the last two elections would undermine Sisi’s legitimacy. That is why the Sisi government has gone to great pains to place several competitors on the ballot and ensure that Sisi doesn’t run opposed—a large voter turnout would dispel doubts about Sisi’s popularity and speculations of potential [unrest](https://www.crisisgroup.org/middle-east-north-africa/north-africa/egypt/eygpt-in-the-balance).

Sisi himself has, so far, done little campaigning and has not given any television or newspaper interviews. That’s either because he is overwhelmed by multiple challenges not least of which is keeping the Gaza war from spilling over into Egypt or because he is confident that his victory in the election is assured.

Israel’s relentless [bombardment](https://www.aljazeera.com/gallery/2023/11/21/photos-intense-israeli-air-strikes-hit-gaza-amid-growing-signs-of-truce) of the besieged Gaza Strip has been both a blessing and a curse for Sisi. It has either dented his popularity or earned him greater support—depending on who you talk to. Some Egyptians are utterly [dismayed](https://twitter.com/Rawanyehia98/status/1713241430674542973https:/twitter.com/Rawanyehia98/status/1713241430674542973) with the government’s handling of the conflict raging on Egypt’s northern border and have called for the permanent opening of the Rafah border crossing to allow Palestinians to [flee](https://www.youtube.com/watch?si=GXI0xMZyA_4Fx1h1&v=9pGCNNjkAfQ&feature=youtu.be) the violence.

Critics see Sisi as “[complicit](https://twitter.com/huwaidaarraf/status/1486168497881292803?lang=ar-x-fm)” in Israel’s killings of civilians and feel helpless and ashamed that Egypt stood idly by and allowed it to happen. Others applaud him for standing firm and not allowing Egypt to be drawn into the conflict. They commend his role in [overseeing](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/menasource/gaza-israel-sisi-egypt-rafah-border/) the flow of humanitarian aid into Gaza and negotiating alongside Qatar and the United States to secure the release of hostages held captive by Hamas in exchange for Palestinian detainees. They also [praise](https://twitter.com/Khalede50601843/status/1719601216731107612?t=4W9bqCNqeF65XpvFdn6IJg&s=03) him for what they view as foiling an [Israeli](https://english.ahram.org.eg/NewsContent/1/1234/512971/Egypt/Foreign-Affairs/Israel-implements-a-plan-to-displace-Palestinians-.aspx) scheme to displace Palestinians into Egypt—despite this not having ever been Israeli policy.

The Gaza war has polarized the already divided country even further. While it is certain that Sisi will win a third term in the election, it is uncertain what will happen after the vote and when the war is over. **Abdel Fattah Saeed Hussein Khalil el-Sisi**[[a]](#cite_note-2) (born 19 November 1954) is an Egyptian politician and retired military officer who has served as the 6th [president of Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Egypt "President of Egypt") since 2014.[[2]](#cite_note-:5-3)

After the [2011 Egyptian revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Egyptian_revolution "2011 Egyptian revolution") and [2012 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Egyptian_presidential_election "2012 Egyptian presidential election") of [Mohamed Morsi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Morsi "Mohamed Morsi") to the Egyptian presidency, the first democratic election in the history of the country, Sisi was appointed Minister of Defense and Commander-in-Chief of the [Egyptian Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian_Armed_Forces "Egyptian Armed Forces") in August 2012, replacing [Hussein Tantawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Hussein_Tantawi "Mohamed Hussein Tantawi"). Following [large scale protests against Morsi's presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/June_2013_Egyptian_protests "June 2013 Egyptian protests"), Sisi led the [2013 Egyptian coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Egyptian_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "2013 Egyptian coup d'état"), overthrowing Morsi on 3 July 2013. Demonstrations and sit-ins organized by supporters of the [Muslim Brotherhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_Brotherhood_in_Egypt "Muslim Brotherhood in Egypt") and [Egyptian democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy_in_Egypt "Democracy in Egypt") followed.

Under the command of Sisi, two camps of protesters were violently dispersed in Cairo: one at al-Nahda Square and a larger one at [Rabaa al-Adawiya Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabaa_al-Adawiya_Square "Rabaa al-Adawiya Square"), the [Rabaa massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabaa_massacre "Rabaa massacre"), leading to international criticism.[[3]](#cite_note-bbc2014election-4) The [dispersal of pro-Morsi sit-ins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-coup_unrest_in_Egypt_(2013%E2%80%932014) "Post-coup unrest in Egypt (2013–2014)") by the police and military forces resulted in the killing of about 800 to 1000+ protestors and the arrests of almost 19,000.[[4]](#cite_note-5) [Human Rights Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Watch "Human Rights Watch") describes the massacres as [crimes against humanity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimes_against_humanity "Crimes against humanity").[[5]](#cite_note-6)[[6]](#cite_note-:4-7)

After the [2014 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Egyptian_presidential_election "2014 Egyptian presidential election"),[[7]](#cite_note-ao26mar-8) Sisi was sworn into office as [President of Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Egypt "President of Egypt") in June 2014.[[8]](#cite_note-9) Sisi faced minimal opposition in the [2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Egyptian_presidential_election "2018 Egyptian presidential election") and [2023 presidential elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Egyptian_presidential_election "2023 Egyptian presidential election"), after other candidates were barred from running or boycotted the election due to repression.[[9]](#cite_note-10)[[10]](#cite_note-11)[[11]](#cite_note-12)[[12]](#cite_note-13) Most independent observers view Sisi as a [dictator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dictator "Dictator").[[13]](#cite_note-dictator-14)[[14]](#cite_note-15) He leads an [authoritarian government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authoritarianism "Authoritarianism") and, according to Human Rights Watch, "relies on naked coercion and the military and security services as his main vehicles of control".[[15]](#cite_note-Truex_&_Tavana_2019-16)[[16]](#cite_note-foreignpolicy-17)[[17]](#cite_note-:1-18)[[18]](#cite_note-19)[[19]](#cite_note-:6-20) Elements of his rule have been described as even more draconian than that of prior authoritarian leader [Hosni Mubarak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hosni_Mubarak "Hosni Mubarak"), who was president from 1981 to 2011.[[20]](#cite_note-21)[[21]](#cite_note-22) In 2024, Egyptian citizens and activists organised an online "Dignity Revolution", resulting in widespread anti-regime protests.[[22]](#cite_note-23)[[23]](#cite_note-:2-24)[[24]](#cite_note-:3-25)[[25]](#cite_note-:0-26) Sisi's government heavily cracked down on dissent in response, arbitrarily detaining hundreds.[[25]](#cite_note-:0-26) Analysts have described Egypt under Sisi as "The [Sick Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sick_man_of_Europe "Sick man of Europe") of the Middle East" due to his fragile rule and Egypt's [economic turbulence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Egypt "Economy of Egypt").[[19]](#cite_note-:6-20)[[26]](#cite_note-27)[[27]](#cite_note-28)

## Early life and military education

Sisi was born in the Gamaleya neighbourhood of [Historic Cairo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historic_Cairo "Historic Cairo")[[28]](#cite_note-29) on 19 November 1954[[29]](#cite_note-30) to Said Hussein Khalil al-Sisi and Soad Ibrahim Mohamed,[[30]](#cite_note-31)[[31]](#cite_note-32)[[32]](#cite_note-33) both from [Monufia Governorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monufia_Governorate "Monufia Governorate").[[33]](#cite_note-34) He grew up in Gamaleya, near [al-Azhar Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Azhar_Mosque "Al-Azhar Mosque"), in a quarter where [Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslims "Muslims"), [Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_Egypt "History of the Jews in Egypt") and [Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity_in_Egypt "Christianity in Egypt") resided and in which he later recalled how, during his childhood, he had heard [church bells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_bell "Church bell") and watched Jews flock to [synagogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synagogue "Synagogue") unhindered.[[34]](#cite_note-35)

He later enrolled in the [Egyptian Military Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian_Military_Academy "Egyptian Military Academy"), and upon graduating he held [various command positions](#Main_command_positions) in the [Egyptian Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian_Armed_Forces "Egyptian Armed Forces") and served as Egypt's [military attaché](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_attach%C3%A9 "Military attaché") in [Riyadh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riyadh "Riyadh"). In 1987, he attended the Egyptian Command and Staff College. In 1992, he continued his military career by enrolling in the British [Command and Staff College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Services_Command_and_Staff_College "Joint Services Command and Staff College"), and, in 2006, enrolled in the [United States Army War College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_War_College "United States Army War College") in Carlisle, Pennsylvania.[[35]](#cite_note-Fast-36) Sisi was the youngest member of the [Supreme Council of the Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Council_of_the_Armed_Forces "Supreme Council of the Armed Forces") (SCAF) during the [Egyptian Revolution of 2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian_Revolution_of_2011 "Egyptian Revolution of 2011"), serving as the director of military intelligence and reconnaissance department. He was later chosen to replace [Mohamed Hussein Tantawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Hussein_Tantawi "Mohamed Hussein Tantawi") and serve as the commander-in-chief and Minister of Defense and Military Production on 12 August 2012.[[36]](#cite_note-37)

Sisi's family origins were in the [Monufia Governorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monufia_Governorate "Monufia Governorate"). He is the second eldest of eight siblings. His father, a conservative Muslim, who later had six additional children with a second wife,[[37]](#cite_note-38) owned an antiques shop for tourists in the historic [bazaar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bazaar "Bazaar") of [Khan el-Khalili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khan_el-Khalili "Khan el-Khalili").[[38]](#cite_note-39)

Sisi and his siblings studied at the nearby library at [al-Azhar University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Azhar_University "Al-Azhar University"). Unlike his brothers—one of whom is a senior judge, another a civil servant—Sisi went to a local army-run secondary school, where he developed a relationship with his maternal cousin, [Entissar Amer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entissar_Amer "Entissar Amer"). They were married upon Sisi's graduation from the Egyptian Military Academy in 1977.[[39]](#cite_note-40)[[40]](#cite_note-41)[[41]](#cite_note-42)[[42]](#cite_note-43)[[43]](#cite_note-44)[[44]](#cite_note-45)[[45]](#cite_note-46) He attended the following courses:

* General Command and Staff Course, Egyptian Command and Staff College, 1987;[[46]](#cite_note-MilitaryEducation-47)
* General Command and Staff Course, [Joint Command and Staff College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Services_Command_and_Staff_College "Joint Services Command and Staff College"), United Kingdom, 1992;[[46]](#cite_note-MilitaryEducation-47)
* War Course, Fellowship of the Higher War College, [Nasser Military Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasser_Military_Academy "Nasser Military Academy"), Egypt, 2003;[[46]](#cite_note-MilitaryEducation-47)
* War Course, [United States Army War College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_War_College "United States Army War College"), United States, 2006;[[46]](#cite_note-MilitaryEducation-47)
* [Egyptian Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian_Armed_Forces "Egyptian Armed Forces") [military attaché](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_attach%C3%A9 "Military attaché") in [Riyadh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riyadh "Riyadh"), [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KSA "KSA");[[46]](#cite_note-MilitaryEducation-47)
* Basic Infantry Course, United States[[46]](#cite_note-MilitaryEducation-47)

## Military career (1977–2014)

Sisi received his commission as a military officer in 1977, serving in the [mechanised infantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanised_infantry "Mechanised infantry") and specialising in [anti-tank warfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-tank_warfare "Anti-tank warfare") and [mortar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortar_(weapon) "Mortar (weapon)") warfare. ### Minister of Defense

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Abdel_Fattah_El-Sisi.jpg/250px-Abdel_Fattah_El-Sisi.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Abdel_Fattah_El-Sisi.jpg)

Abdel Fattah el-Sisi's official portrait as [Minister of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Defense_(Egypt) "Ministry of Defense (Egypt)"), 2014

On 12 August 2012, Egyptian President [Mohamed Morsi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Morsi "Mohamed Morsi") made a decision to replace the Mubarak-era [Field Marshal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Marshal "Field Marshal") [Mohamed Hussein Tantawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Hussein_Tantawi "Mohamed Hussein Tantawi"), the head of the [Egyptian Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian_Armed_Forces "Egyptian Armed Forces"), with then little-known Sisi. He also promoted him to the rank of [colonel general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonel_general "Colonel general").[[50]](#cite_note-51) Sisi was then described by the official website of the ruling [Muslim Brotherhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_Brotherhood "Muslim Brotherhood")-aligned [Freedom and Justice Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_and_Justice_Party_(Egypt) "Freedom and Justice Party (Egypt)") as a "defense minister with revolutionary taste".[[51]](#cite_note-52) Sisi also took the post of Minister of Defense and Military Production in the [Qandil Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qandil_Cabinet "Qandil Cabinet").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/Secretary_of_Defense_Chuck_Hagel_meets_with_Egyptian_President_Mohamed_Morsy_in_Cairo%2C_Egypt%2C_April_24%2C_2013.jpg/250px-Secretary_of_Defense_Chuck_Hagel_meets_with_Egyptian_President_Mohamed_Morsy_in_Cairo%2C_Egypt%2C_April_24%2C_2013.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Secretary_of_Defense_Chuck_Hagel_meets_with_Egyptian_President_Mohamed_Morsy_in_Cairo,_Egypt,_April_24,_2013.jpg)

General al-Sisi (left) and then President Mohamed Morsi (right) listen to visiting U.S. Secretary of Defense [Chuck Hagel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Hagel "Chuck Hagel") (centre) during a meeting with U.S. officials on 24 April 2013, just months before Sisi overthrew Morsi in a coup d'état.

Sisi was appointed as Minister of Defense on 12 August 2012. He remained in office under the new government formed after the deposition of Morsi, and led by [Hazem al-Beblawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazem_al-Beblawi "Hazem al-Beblawi"). He was also appointed Deputy Prime Minister of Egypt. On 27 January 2014, he was promoted to the rank of [field marshal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_marshal "Field marshal").[[52]](#cite_note-53)

### Coup d'état and Rabaa massacre

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Anti-Morsi_protest_poster_june_2013.jpg/250px-Anti-Morsi_protest_poster_june_2013.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Anti-Morsi_protest_poster_june_2013.jpg)

Demonstrations against President Morsi, June 2013

Mass demonstrations occurred on 30 June 2013 as Egyptians took to the streets to protest policies of the democratically-elected Morsi government. Soon afterwards, the [Egyptian Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian_Army "Egyptian Army") issued a 48-hour ultimatum which aired on television that gave the country's political parties until 3 July to meet their demands. The Egyptian military also threatened to intervene if the dispute was not resolved by then.[[53]](#cite_note-alprofile-54)

On 3 July 2013, the Egyptian Armed Forces initiated a coup d'état. The army then installed the Chief Justice of the Supreme Constitutional Court [Adly Mansour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adly_Mansour "Adly Mansour") as the interim head of state in his place until a new president could be elected, and ordered the arrest of many members of the Muslim Brotherhood on charges of "inciting violence and disturbing general security and peace".[[54]](#cite_note-businessinsider-55) Sisi announced on television that the president had "failed to meet the demands of the Egyptian people" and declared that the constitution would be temporarily suspended, which was met by acceptance from anti-Morsi protesters and condemnation from pro-Morsi supporters in Rabaa al-Adawiya.

On 24 July 2013, during a speech at a military parade, Sisi called for mass demonstrations to grant the [Egyptian military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian_Army "Egyptian Army") and [police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian_National_Police "Egyptian National Police") a "mandate" to crack down on pro-democracy protestors.[[55]](#cite_note-56) While supporters interpreted this to mean that Sisi felt the need of the people to prove to the world that it was not a coup but the popular will, the statement was seen by opponents as contradicting the military's pledges to hand over power to civilians after removing Morsi and as indicating an imminent crackdown against [Islamists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamists "Islamists").[[56]](#cite_note-NewYorkTimes-57)[[57]](#cite_note-BBC-58)

The reactions to Sisi's announcement ranged from open support from the interim [Egyptian presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Egypt "President of Egypt")[[58]](#cite_note-59) and the [Tamarod movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamarod "Tamarod")[[59]](#cite_note-60) to rejection by much of civil society, the [Muslim Brotherhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_Brotherhood_in_Egypt "Muslim Brotherhood in Egypt"),[[56]](#cite_note-NewYorkTimes-57) the Salafi [Nour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nour_Party "Nour Party"),[[60]](#cite_note-Nour-61) the [Strong Egypt Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_Egypt_Party "Strong Egypt Party"),[[61]](#cite_note-62) the liberal [April 6 Youth Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_6_Youth_Movement "April 6 Youth Movement")[[62]](#cite_note-63) and human rights groups.[[63]](#cite_note-64)

During the dispersal process of anti-coup protestors, the Egyptian military under Sisi's command was involved in assisting the [national police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian_National_Police "Egyptian National Police") in dispersing two sit-ins held by anti-coup protestors in Rabaa el-Adaweya and Nahda squares. This action resulted in led to [murder of over 900 protestors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_2013_Rabaa_Massacre#Casualties "August 2013 Rabaa Massacre") by Egyptian security forces in the [Rabaa Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabaa_massacre "Rabaa massacre").[[6]](#cite_note-:4-7)[[64]](#cite_note-ahram1-65)[[65]](#cite_note-66) [Human Rights Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Watch "Human Rights Watch") described the sit-in dispersals as [crimes against humanity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimes_against_humanity "Crimes against humanity") and called them "one of the world's largest killings of demonstrators in a single day in recent history."[[66]](#cite_note-Hrw.org-67) In 2023, [Amnesty International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International "Amnesty International") released stated that, "The 10-year anniversary of the Rabaa massacre is a stark reminder of how impunity for the mass killing of over 900 people has enabled an all-out assault on peaceful dissent, an erosion of any fair trial safeguards in the criminal justice system, and unspeakable cruelty in prisons over the past decade, Amnesty International said today."[[67]](#cite_note-68)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/R4bia_sign_used_in_solidarity_with_victims_of_Rabaa_crackdown_23-Aug-2013.jpg/250px-R4bia_sign_used_in_solidarity_with_victims_of_Rabaa_crackdown_23-Aug-2013.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:R4bia_sign_used_in_solidarity_with_victims_of_Rabaa_crackdown_23-Aug-2013.jpg)

Muslim Brotherhood supporters protesting against Sisi in solidarity with the victims of the Rabaa Massacre in Cairo, August 2013

Writing for British newspaper *[The Independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Independent "The Independent")* in August 2013, [Robert Fisk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Fisk "Robert Fisk") described then-General Sisi as being at a loss, but that a massacre—as Fisk called the sit-in dispersal—would go down in history as an infamy.[[68]](#cite_note-69) Writing for the American magazine *[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")*, Lee Smith concluded that "Egypt's new leader [was] unfit to rule", referring not to the actual head of government at the time, interim president [Adly Mansour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adly_Mansour "Adly Mansour"), but to Sisi.[[69]](#cite_note-70)

In a file published by the State Information Services, the government explained the raids by stating that "police went on to use force dispersing the sit-in on 14 August 2013 with the least possible damage, causing hundreds of civilians and police to fall as victims, while [Muslim Brotherhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_Brotherhood "Muslim Brotherhood") supporters imposed a blockade for 46 days against the people in al-Nahda and Rabaa al-Adawiya squares under the name of sit-in where tens of protesters took to the street daily hindered the lives of the Egyptians, causing unrest and the death or injury of many victims as well as damage to public and private properties".[[70]](#cite_note-71)

On 3 August 2013, Sisi gave his first interview since the overthrow of Mohamed Morsi. Speaking to *[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post "The Washington Post")*, he criticised the US response, and accused the [Obama administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obama_administration "Obama administration") of disregarding the Egyptian popular will and of providing insufficient support amid threats of a civil war, saying, "You left the Egyptians. You turned your back on the Egyptians and they won't forget that."[[71]](#cite_note-72)

On the 40th anniversary of the [Yom Kippur War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yom_Kippur_War "Yom Kippur War") (also known as the October War) on 6 October 2013, Sisi called for the "[unification of Arabs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan-Arabism "Pan-Arabism")" during a ceremony attended by the ministers of defence of the UAE, Bahrain, Morocco, Jordan and Iraq. He declared the Egyptian army's solidarity with anti-Morsi rallies and commented that the relationship between the army and people was "hard to break", adding: "We would die before you [the Egyptian people] would feel pain". He also compared the army to the [Great Pyramid of Giza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza "Great Pyramid of Giza"), saying that "it cannot be broken".[[72]](#cite_note-dailynewsegypt.com-73)

#### Civil liberties

After Sisi had removed Morsi from office and disbanded the [Egyptian Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_(Egypt) "Senate (Egypt)"), in September 2013 interim president Adly Mansour temporarily decreed that ministers could award contracts without a [request for tender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Request_for_tender "Request for tender"). In the next month, the government awarded building contracts worth approximately one billion dollars to the Egyptian Army.[[73]](#cite_note-kingsley_list-74) In April 2014, the interim government's Investment Law banned appeals against government contracts.

Also in September 2013, the interim government removed pre-trial detention limits for certain crimes, allowing certain individuals remain [in detention indefinitely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indefinite_detention_without_trial "Indefinite detention without trial"). In November 2013, the interim government temporarily banned protests in an attempt to combat the growing pro-Brotherhood unrest; the police arrested thousands of Egyptians using the new law.[[73]](#cite_note-kingsley_list-74)

On 24 March 2014, an Egyptian court sentenced 529 members of the Muslim Brotherhood [to death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment "Capital punishment"),[[74]](#cite_note-75) following an attack on a police station in 2013, an act described by [Amnesty International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International "Amnesty International") as "the largest single batch of simultaneous death sentences we've seen in recent years [...] anywhere in the world".[[75]](#cite_note-76) The [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC") reported that by May 2016, approximately 40,000 people, mostly Brotherhood members or loyalists, had been imprisoned since Morsi's overthrow.[[76]](#cite_note-77)

Presidential elections were held in [Egypt](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt "Egypt") in December 2023, as announced by the National Election Authority,[[2]](#cite_note-es25sept-2) after speculation that the elections might be held earlier than expected.[[3]](#cite_note-3) Candidate registration was from 5–14 October 2023 and the election was held in Egypt from 10 to 12 December;[[2]](#cite_note-es25sept-2) expatriates voted from 1–3 December.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Incumbent president [Abdel Fattah el-Sisi](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdel_Fattah_el-Sisi "Abdel Fattah el-Sisi"), who initially came to power in the aftermath of the [2013 Egyptian coup d'état](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Egyptian_coup_d'état "2013 Egyptian coup d'état"), was eligible for re-election since term limits were adjusted from four to six years by a [constitutional amendment in 2019](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Egyptian_constitutional_referendum "2019 Egyptian constitutional referendum"), and he technically will not have served as president for more than the maximum of 12 years at the time of the election. His rule has been described as [authoritarian](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authoritarian "Authoritarian").[[1]](#cite_note-expect-1)[[5]](#cite_note-Truex_&_Tavana_2019-5)[[6]](#cite_note-foreignpolicy-6)[[7]](#cite_note-hrw-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9) On 18 December he was reported to have won with 90% of the vote with a 67% turnout.[[10]](#cite_note-10) El-Sisi was inaugurated for another term on 2 April 2024, with his victory attributed to him facing no serious challengers.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

Incumbent president el-Sisi won the [2018 elections](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Egyptian_presidential_election "2018 Egyptian presidential election") with over 97% of the vote, and faced only nominal opposition (a pro-government supporter, [Moussa Mostafa Moussa](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moussa_Mostafa_Moussa "Moussa Mostafa Moussa")) after several opposition figures were prevented from participating following the military arrest of [Sami Anan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sami_Hafez_Anan "Sami Hafez Anan"),[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13)[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15) threats made to [Ahmed Shafik](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmed_Shafik "Ahmed Shafik") with old corruption charges and an alleged [sex tape](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur_pornography "Amateur pornography"),[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18) and the withdrawal of [Khaled Ali](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khaled_Ali "Khaled Ali") and [Mohamed Anwar El-Sadat](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Anwar_Esmat_Sadat "Mohamed Anwar Esmat Sadat") due to the overwhelming obstacles presented, and violations committed, by the elections committee.[[19]](#cite_note-19)[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21)

Since 2022 Egypt had been in the midst of an economic crisis, including record high inflation causing the [Egyptian pound](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian_pound "Egyptian pound") to lose nearly half its value from March 2022 to January 2023[[22]](#cite_note-22) and a shortage of foreign currency, the latter of which driven in part by the [Russian invasion of Ukraine](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "Russian invasion of Ukraine"). Prior to the crisis, roughly 30% of the population was already living below the poverty line, with an additional 30% considered vulnerable to poverty. Furthermore, the country's external debt bill tripled in the ten years prior.[[23]](#cite_note-23) Egypt had put several state-owned companies and stakes [up for sale](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privatization "Privatization") in a bid to raise money, and about half of the 2023/24 budget is allocated to debt servicing. The [IMF](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund "International Monetary Fund") has also requested that the Egyptian pound transition to a fully [floating exchange rate](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating_exchange_rate "Floating exchange rate") in order for a round of loans to be released. Government spending on projects without a return on investment, such as the [New Administrative Capital](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Administrative_Capital "New Administrative Capital"), were also blamed for contributing,[[24]](#cite_note-24) in addition to a persistent trade deficit and continuing influence of the military in economic affairs.[[25]](#cite_note-25)[[26]](#cite_note-26) [Moody's](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moody's_Investors_Service "Moody's Investors Service") labeled Egypt as one of the top five economies most at risk of defaulting on foreign debt in 2023.[[27]](#cite_note-27)

The [president of Egypt](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Egypt "President of Egypt") is elected using the [two-round system](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-round_system "Two-round system") for a term of six years, renewable once.[[28]](#cite_note-28)

To participate, a candidate can either secure the endorsement of 20 MPs or "25,000 eligible voters across at least 15 governorates," with at least 1,000 endorsements from each governorate.[[29]](#cite_note-ahramweekly3oct-29) Additionally, per Article 141 of the constitution:[[30]](#cite_note-30)

* A candidate must be an Egyptian citizen born to Egyptian parents
* The candidate, their parents, and their spouse must not hold dual citizenship
* The candidate must not have been denied their civil and political rights due to a criminal conviction

![](https://www.eipr.org/sites/default/files/styles/article_image_feature_small/public/images/photo-library/untitled2_0_0.png?itok=gLXXJ5Rk&timestamp=1694860279)

### Press Release

16 September 2023

**The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR) said the National Security Sector (NSS) arrested at least 35 volunteers in the campaign of presidential hopeful Ahmed Tantawi in 13 governorates over the last three weeks.**

**Some of the volunteers were arrested from their homes, workplaces or while on their way to meet Tantawi, while others were summoned to the closest National Security offices where they were detained.**

**After several days of detention in undisclosed places, th NSS moved them to Cairo and brought them before the Supreme State Security Prosecution, which charged them with “membership of a subversive organization” and disseminating false news, and remanded them all in custody.**

**The EIPR documented the names of 35 volunteers who were arrested and detained in different governorates as follows: Gharbia (5), Minya (5), Cairo (4), Giza (3), Qena (3), Sohag (3), Dakahlia (3), Menoufia (3), Sharqia (2), Damietta (1), Alexandria (1), Kafr El-Sheikh (1) and Qalyubia (1).**

**The crackdown began on or around 25 August, but most volunteers were arrested after being summoned to National Security offices in different governorates on the evening of 12 September. A source in Tantawi's campaign said the whereabouts of some of those arrested are still unknown.**

**The EIPR said that 29 of those arrested were brought before the Supreme State Security Prosecution in New Cairo on 14 September. EIPR lawyers attended the interrogation sessions with a number of them. The prosecution did not present the detainees with any specific incidents or evidence, nor were they questioned about Tantawi's campaign. However, the detainees stated that they were interrogated at NSS solely about the reasons they filled their data in an online volunteering form that Tantawi’s campaign had posted about two months earlier. All the detainees were transferred to the 10th of Ramadan Prison pending investigation into Case No. 2123 of 2023 (Supreme State Security).**

**The EIPR strongly condemned this unlawful crackdown, which targets citizens not even because of their peaceful political activism, but simply for expressing their intention to legally engage in the campaign of an opposition candidate. The launch of this nationwide, coordinated crackdown even before the National Election Authority opens the door of candidacy in the upcoming presidential elections leaves no doubt about the intentions of the security services (and the complicity of the State Security Prosecution - to shield the president from any potential competition or even campaigns of his rivals, just as happened in the last infamous elections in 2018.**

**The EIPR calls for the immediate release of the detained volunteers and urges the judiciary and the National Election Authority to assume their constitutional responsibility for protecting citizens’ right to political participation.**

Contents of https://www.hrw.org/news/2023/05/05/egypt-mass-arrests-target-family-supporters-ex-mp:
(Beirut) – The [Egyptian](https://www.hrw.org/middle-east/n-africa/egypt) authorities have since late April 2023 arrested at least 12 family members and perceived supporters of Ahmed Tantawy, a former parliament member who said in March that he would run for president in the 2024 elections, Human Rights Watch said today.

The arrests appear to be solely based on the individuals’ relationship with Tantawy, preempting his announcement that he would return to Egypt from abroad on May 6. The authorities should immediately release all those detained merely for exercising their basic rights to free association and expression or because of their relationship with Tantawy, and present anyone for whom there is evidence of wrongdoing before a judge to review the legality and necessity of their detention.

“The arrests of relatives and supporters of Ahmed Tantawy demonstrate that President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s government is determined to stifle peaceful dissent and label all critics as threats,” said [Amr Magdi](https://www.hrw.org/about/people/amr-magdi), senior Middle East and North Africa researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Such abuses infringe on the rights of those targeted and severely reduce the country’s prospects for democratic and human rights for many years to come.”

Lawyers told Human Rights Watch that the authorities arrested two of Tantawy’s uncles at their homes in Kafr el-Sheikh, a city north of Cairo, on May 2 and 3. The lawyers said that security forces also arrested at least 10 other men perceived to be supportive or friends of Tantawy. Prosecutors ordered the detention of all 12 people for 15 days pending investigation [on the charge](https://twitter.com/Khaledali251/status/1654215309434187778) of “joining a terrorist group,” while some of them faced additional charges of financing that group, “possessing publications that undermine public security,” and possessing fireworks, explosives, or firearms.

An Egyptian human rights lawyer, Nasser Amin, [tweeted](https://twitter.com/NasserAmi/status/1654127814894055436) that some of those arrested have been in custody since April. Tantawy said in [a Facebook video](https://fb.watch/kjXWcAXvxJ/?mibextid=2Rb1fB) on May 5, recorded in Lebanon, where he has been living for several months, that this arrest campaign is the third time authorities have targeted his family and supporters to silence him in recent months.

Tantawy announced that he plans to return to Egypt on May 6 and run for president in 2024. He is the former head of the leftist al-Karama Party, and was one of the very few critical voices between 2015 and 2019 in the parliament, which was and remains overwhelmingly dominated by supporters of the president.

In August 2022, Tantawy left Egypt for Lebanon after he [resigned](https://www.almasryalyoum.com/news/details/2644010) from the al-Karama Party. Members of his party said in local media [reports](https://www.madamasr.com/ar/2022/08/13/news/u/%D8%A3%D8%AD%D9%85%D8%AF-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B7%D9%86%D8%B7%D8%A7%D9%88%D9%8A-%D9%8A%D8%BA%D8%A7%D8%AF%D8%B1-%D8%A5%D9%84%D9%89-%D8%A8%D9%8A%D8%B1%D9%88%D8%AA-%D9%88%D9%85%D8%B5%D8%AF%D8%B1%D8%A7%D9%86/) that he resigned and left Egypt under pressure from security agencies. “When the closest and most beloved people in my social circle are harmed, this is definitely a type of indirect pressure. It is definitely painful,” Tantawy said [in a BBC interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eAYKrt1WHz0) in September. Security forces have in recent years [arrested](https://www.ec-rf.net/%D8%A8%D9%8A%D8%A7%D9%86-%D8%B5%D8%AD%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%A8%D8%B4%D8%A3%D9%86-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%82%D8%A8%D8%B6-%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%89-%D8%A3%D8%B9%D8%B6%D8%A7%D8%A1-%D8%AD%D8%B2%D8%A8-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%83%D8%B1/) several members of the party over their political activities.

Human Rights Watch has documented a clear pattern of Egyptian authorities’ [reprisals against families](https://www.hrw.org/news/2021/02/19/egypt-escalating-reprisals-arrests-critics-families) in Egypt of activists and critics living abroad, using unlawful home raids, arbitrary arrests, enforced disappearances, and prolonged detention of family members without trial or charges.

Two lawyers who attended the prosecution interrogation session with the two uncles, Mohamed Naguib Tantawy and Mohamed Sayed Attia, said that National Security agents held the two at a National Security Agency building in Kafr el-Shiekh for about 24 hours with no communication with the outside world before taking them to the Supreme State Security Prosecution in Cairo.

The lawyers said that prosecutors ordered the uncles detained for 15 days on Security Agency allegations that the men, ages 71 and 61, were distributing publications calling on people to meet Tantawy at Cairo airport upon his arrival on May 6 and use “force” to release him if security arrested him.

The National Security Agency is an Interior Ministry division [involved in widespread abuses](https://www.hrw.org/report/2017/09/05/we-do-unreasonable-things-here/torture-and-national-security-al-sisis-egypt), some of which have most likely amounted to [crimes against humanity](https://www.hrw.org/news/2017/09/06/egypt-torture-epidemic-may-be-crime-against-humanity). Members of the Supreme State Security Prosecutions in Egypt [typically remand people in custody for months or years](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/press-release/2019/11/egypt-state-security-prosecution-operating-as-a-sinister-tool-of-repression/) without trial, and frequently base their decisions on unsubstantiated security allegations. International human rights law necessitates taking anyone detained before a judge or the equivalent, not a prosecutor, swiftly – within 48 hours – to review their detention and assess whether they should be released.

Lawyers said that prosecutors presented 20 pieces of fireworks and 70 leaflets as the material evidence to support the detention of Tantawy’s uncles. The lawyers said that security forces who arrested one of the uncles knocked on his door at dawn, asked for his national identification document, and then escorted him away without searching his home.

President al-Sisi won 97 percent of votes in [unfair and unfree](https://web.archive.org/web/20201127174346/https:/www.hrw.org/news/2018/02/13/egypt-planned-presidential-vote-neither-free-nor-fair) presidential elections in 2018. In the weeks and months before the election, the authorities [successively eliminated key challengers](https://www.hrw.org/news/2018/02/13/egypt-planned-presidential-vote-neither-free-nor-fair) who announced their intention to run for president by arresting two of them, placing one under house arrest, and pushing another two to withdraw due to concerns over the safety of their supporters and government manipulation. In the end, al-Sisi ran against [one of his own](https://www.reuters.com/article/us-egypt-election-result-idUSKCN1H916A) supporters with no real competition.

“There will be no fair or free elections in Egypt as long as authorities continue to stifle basic freedoms and crush the rule of law to intimidate critics,” Magdi said.
